Bumps [Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn) from 4.5.0 to 4.6.0.
Release notes

Sourced from Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp's releases.

.NET 6.0.1

Release

.NET 5.0.4

Release

.NET 5.0.2

Release Notes Install Instructions

Repos

  • Core
Changelog

Sourced from Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp's changelog.

API Breaking Changes

Version 1.1.0

Removed VisualBasicCommandLineParser.ctor

During a toolset update we noticed the constructor on VisualBasicCommandLineParser was public. This in turn made many of the protected members of CommandLineParser a part of the API surface as it gave external customers an inheritance path.

It was never the intent for these members to be a part of the supported API surface. Creation of the parsers is meant to be done via the Default singleton properties. There seems to be little risk that we broke any customers here and hence we decided to remove this API.

PR: dotnet/roslyn#4169

Changed Simplifier methods to throw ArgumentNullExceptions

Changed Simplifier.ReduceAsync, Simplifier.ExpandAsync, and Simplifier.Expand methods to throw ArgumentNullExceptions if any non-optional, nullable arguments are passed in. Previously the user would get a NullReferenceException for synchronous methods and an AggregateException containing a NullReferenceException for asynchronous methods.

PR: dotnet/roslyn#5144

Version 1.3.0

Treat a method marked with both public and private flags as private

The scenario is loading an assembly where some methods, fields or nested types have accessibility flags set to 7 (all three bits set), which mean public AND private. After the fix, such flags are loaded to mean private. The compat change is we’re trading a compile-time success and runtime failure (native compiler) against a compile-time error (restoring the behavior of v1.2).

Details below:

  • The native compiler successfully compiles the method and field case (those only yield runtime error System.TypeLoadException: Invalid Field Access Flags) and reported an accessibility error on the nested type.
  • The 1.2 compiler generated errors:
error BC30390: 'C.Private Overloads Sub M()' is not accessible in this context because it is 'Private'.
error BC30389: 'C.F' is not accessible in this context because it is 'Private'.
error BC30389: 'C.C2' is not accessible in this context because it is 'Protected Friend'.
error BC30390: 'C2.Private Overloads Sub M2()' is not accessible in this context because it is 'Private'.
  • The 1.3 compiler crashes.
  • After fix, the same errors as 1.2 are generated again.

PR: dotnet/roslyn#11547

Don't emit bad DateTimeConstant, and load bad BadTimeConstant as default value instead

The change affects compatibility in two ways:

  • When loading an invalid DateTimeConstant(-1), the compiler will use default(DateTime) instead, whereas the native compiler would produce code that fails to execute.
  • DateTimeConstant(-1) will still count when we check that you don’t specify two default values. The compiler will produce an error, instead of succeeding (and producing IL with two attributes).

body:
Do you recall why the decision was made to set the backupFocusedControl to null on the following line instead of calling this.RestoreFocus() ?

https://github.com/fluentribbon/Fluent.Ribbon/blob/10d353ea0250d6f9baac6a06681e9db6c8144f30/Fluent.Ribbon/Services/KeyTipService.cs#LL290C37-L290C37

I have a user who is attempting to remap the Left key to Alt+H using Power Toys (see https://github.com/DaxStudio/DaxStudio/issues/1137) and I think I've been able to track the issue down to the fact that the line above does not restore the focus. I was able to replicate the issue in the showcase app and setting the above line to `this.RestoreFocus();` "fixed" the issue, but because I don't understand why the focus was not being restored in the first place I'm not sure what other side effects this change might have.

If this "fix" is overly simplistic I could just go down the route of adding an option to my app to set IsKeyTipHandlingEnabled ="False" - It's a bit of a drastic step, but I don't think it's worth wasting too much time on this issue as I don't see it as an overly common issue.

---
### Environment

- Fluent.Ribbon __v?.?.?__
- Windows 11
- .NET Framework 4.7.2

body:
The "BackButton" on the Backstage has a flaw, that it mixes languages and the localization is "not ideal".

This button here:
![image](https://github.com/fluentribbon/Fluent.Ribbon/assets/756703/8e239e25-7c79-45f1-b55b-005f9e561f92) 
... work with a screenreader since [this change](https://github.com/fluentribbon/Fluent.Ribbon/issues/1125). 

Unfortunately the German translation is "not ideal", because of the Wording "Backstage schließen".
"Backstage" itself is used by Microsoft even in German support sites, but our accessibility tester doesn't allow this, because NVDA, Jaws & the Windows Narrator have a weird pronunciation of it.

I checked if I could change the title myself to "Menü schließen", which doesn't sound too bad, but the screenreader will read "Menü schließen - Button - Open Backstage", which is weird.

The "Open Backstage" originates from the RoutedUICommand:

![image](https://github.com/fluentribbon/Fluent.Ribbon/assets/756703/afba7aac-1297-4050-8876-ffc1c4718636), which is currently hardcoded:

```
public static class RibbonCommands
{
    /// <summary>
    /// Gets the value that represents the Open Backstage command
    /// </summary>
    public static readonly RoutedCommand OpenBackstage = new RoutedUICommand("Open backstage", nameof(OpenBackstage), typeof(RibbonCommands));
}
```

The "easiest" fix would be to change the "Backstage" to "Menü" (for the German translation) and somehow use the same text for the RoutedUICommand, but I'm not even sure if this is needed or if the text could be removed anyway.

---
### Environment

- Fluent.Ribbon __v10__
- Windows __11__
- .NET Framework __4.8__
title: RibbonBackButton - Localization Mix

body:
Hi!
I found a potential issue in the definition of the maximum height of a dropdown of the DropDown buttons.
The dependency property is defined as follows:

`public static readonly DependencyProperty MaxDropDownHeightProperty =
        DependencyProperty.Register(nameof(MaxDropDownHeight), typeof(double), typeof(DropDownButton), new PropertyMetadata(SystemParameters.PrimaryScreenHeight / 3.0));`

As far as I know, the SystemParameters.PrimaryScreenHeight does not consider DPI settings of the monitors.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.systemparameters.primaryscreenheight?view=windowsdesktop-7.0

In my opinion it is also questionably to use the height of the primary screen as the application could be shown on a different screen with totally different settings.
title: Maximum dropdown height is not screen aware

body:
When Ribbon is used as Content inside BusyIndicator pattern (Content, Overlay rectangle, BusyContent) on Windows 10 'Not enough quota' exception is throwing inside WPF. On Windows 11 all works as expected.

Exception is raised when ContentControl inside RibbonWindow where Ribbon is located received ```false``` value to IsEnabled property.
RibbonWindow->BusyIndicator->Grid->Ribbon

I tested 9,10 Fluent.Ribbon versions - all show same error on Windows 10 (22.H2 10.0.19045.3393)

This can be related to https://github.com/fluentribbon/Fluent.Ribbon/issues/634 
Also I found description of this type of problems [here](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/12584619/mysterious-not-enough-quota-is-available-to-process-this-command-in-winrt-port) and [here](https://social.msdn.microsoft.com/Forums/en-US/d778c6e0-c248-4a1a-9391-28d038247578/mysterious-8220not-enough-quota-is-available-to-process-this-command8221-in-winrt-port-of?forum=winappswithcsharp)
 
For workaround this BusyIndicator should not disable Content, just hide it with overlay rectangle.

Release Notes Install Instructions

Repos

Changelog

Sourced from Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp's changelog.

Version 4.7.0

SymbolDisplayFormat includes parameter name when invoked on IParameterSymbol

All SymbolDisplayFormats (predefined and user-created) now include parameter names by default if used on a standalone IParameterSymbol for consistency with predefined formats (see the breaking change for version 4.5.0 above).

Changed IncrementalStepRunReason when a modified input produced a new output

IncrementalGeneratorRunStep.Outputs previously contained IncrementalStepRunReason.Modified as Reason when the input to the step was modified in a way that produced a new output. Now the reason will be reported more accurately as IncrementalStepRunReason.New.

Version 4.8.0

Changed Assembly.Location behavior in non-Windows

The value of Assembly.Location previously held the location on disk where an analyzer or source generator was loaded from. This could be either the original location or the shadow copy location. In 4.8 this will be "" in certain cases when running on non Windows platforms. This is due the compiler server loading assemblies using AssemblyLoadContext.LoadFromStream instead of loading from disk.

This could already happen in other load scenarios but this change moves it into mainline build scenarios.

body:
Icon property of various controls is considered as a string value that need to be translated by translation tools like catalyst, ..., because of this, an icon property value is listed in the table of strings that needs translation.

Usually a psuedo translation is done on the strings listed by translation tools before sending to professional translators by the development teams to test every text in the application is supported for translation, for example, a value of /Images/xxx.ico with psuedo translation would end up something like 'tr_/images/xxx.ico_tr', since this will break the paths to icons, application will crash. Even with the professional translators, unless they know what these texts are, they could translate to locale they intend to translate something like '/bilder/xxx.ico' for a swedish locale which leads to application crash

Icon property of controls should be marked as non localizable to avoid this.

---
### Environment

- Fluent.Ribbon 10.1.0
- Windows 10
- .NET Framework 4.8
title: Icon property values of controls are translated by the translation tools like catalyst

body:
Pull request for the issue: #1222 

What changed:
Set the [Localizability(LocalizationCategory.NeverLocalize)] and [Localizable(false)] attributes on Icon properties of the controls, so that translation tools do not consider value of Icon property for localizing.

Example:
Before translation
Icon="pack://application:,,,/xxxLibrary;component/Icons/16x16/icnExit.png"

After psuedo translation
Icon="tr_pack://application:,,,/Nmx.Workplace.Library.StyleLibrary;component/Icons/16x16/icnExit.png_tr"
title: Set Icon properties as NonLocalizable

body: After upgrading from v9 to v10 of the Fluent.Ribbon library, we have noticed that the ComboBox control fails to render any items the first time a user is trying to expand the dropdown. Consecutive user interactions render the dropdown content as expected. We tracked this down to the `ItemsPanelTemplate` which we added a while ago (as described here (https://github.com/fluentribbon/Fluent.Ribbon/issues/309)) in order to support grouping of items using a `Fluent:GalleryPanel` (also see code sample below). Note that the issue goes away if we remove the custom `ItemsPanelTemplate `but then we lose the Grouping which we had with Fluent.Ribbon v9. So is this still the recommended way of adding Grouping to comboBox items or is there another way in Fluent.Ribbon v10? ```XAML ``` First click on comboBox shows no items in dropdown: Closing the dropdown and clicking again on comboBox shows dropdown items with Grouping as expected : --- ### Environment - Fluent.Ribbon __v10.1.0__ - Windows __11__ - .NET Framework __4.8__
title: ComboBox dropdown is empty when expanding for the first time when specifying ItemsPanelTemplate in order to add Grouping

body:
The new release includes the breaking change:
```
DropDownButton, SplitButton and ApplicationMenu don't generate MenuItem but ContentPresenter as containers.

This provides more flexibility and also fixes the nested MenuItem issues.
```
 
I adapted simple DropDownButtons to the changes, but for a DropDownButton that has a menu with nested items I could not find a way. As there is no concrete example for this breaking change, I have made a repo to demonstrate the unexpected behavior, having menu items with the arrow but no subsequent menu opening.

Example found under **Tests -> Dropdown (auto close on click)**

https://github.com/imadenis/Fluent.Ribbon.Demo

body:
I'm used to customize the Window menu (i.e. System menu), and I encounter some problems with the version 11 (it seems the version 10 also have some, but less important, issue). I published a small project in https://github.com/YetAnotherCodeMaker/FluentRibbonSamples/tree/main/V11RibbonWindowMenuIssue to show the problem.

You can set the project property `FluentRibbonVersion` to 0, 10 or 11 to generate the application without Fluent Ribbon or with version 10 or 11. This generates a small application with a simple window in which the Window menu can be reverted to its default state by clicking the "Rebuild Window Menu" button (which invokes the Win32 `GetSystemMenu` function and try to get a native handle to it; a border indicates if this handle is null or not).

My analysis is the following (the `ResizeMode` of the Window is set to `CanMiminize`)

### without Fluent Ribbon
#### initial menu
`Restore`, `Size` and `Maximize` are disabled (this is expected)
#### menu after rebuild
same as initial (this is expected too)

### with Fluent Ribbon version 10
#### initial menu
`Restore` and `Size` are disabled, `Maximised` is enabled (while it shouldn't)
#### menu after rebuild
often, the first time the menu is opened, all items are enabled, the initial situation returns from the second time it is opened

### with Fluent Ribbon version 11
#### initial menu
as in version 10
#### menu after rebuild
the menu is empty (a native handle cannot even be retrieved)
title: Version 11 Window Menu issue

body:
## Summary

  Third companion guide to #1259 and #1260, covering a common dark mode issue: button text remaining black (unreadable) against dark backgrounds.

  ## The Problem

  After implementing custom dark mode theming, Fluent.Ribbon button text (Button, DropDownButton, SplitButton) often stays black. Setting `Foreground` via code-behind doesn't work.

  ## What I'm Contributing

  A guide covering:
  - **5 approaches that don't work** and why (code-behind, TextElement.SetForeground, resource overrides, ThemeManager)
  - **Why nothing works** - internal template bindings, StaticResource usage
  - **The simple fix** - XAML `DynamicResource` binding
  - **Complete examples** for buttons, split buttons, dropdowns, and group headers

  ## Key Insight

  Two different theming approaches are needed:
  | Element Type | Approach |
  |-------------|----------|
  | Ribbon structure (panels, borders) | Visual tree walk |
  | Declared controls (buttons) | XAML DynamicResource |

  ---

  <details>
  <summary>Click to expand full guide</summary>

  # Fluent.Ribbon Dark Mode Button Text Guide

**A guide to fixing unreadable button text in dark mode Fluent.Ribbon applications.**

*Tested with Fluent.Ribbon 10.0.4 and 11.0.1 on .NET 8.0 WPF*

---

## Table of Contents

1. [The Problem](#the-problem)
2. [What Doesn't Work](#what-doesnt-work)
3. [Why Nothing Works](#why-nothing-works)
4. [The Solution](#the-solution)
5. [Complete Implementation](#complete-implementation)
6. [Key Insights](#key-insights)

---

## The Problem

After implementing custom dark mode theming for Fluent.Ribbon (tab row colors, backgrounds, etc.), button text often remains black - completely unreadable against dark backgrounds.

**Symptoms:**
- Ribbon button headers (text labels) are black in dark mode
- DropDownButton, SplitButton, ToggleButton text all affected
- Standard WPF controls in the same window show correct light text
- Only Fluent.Ribbon button controls have the issue

**Why it's confusing:**
The `Foreground` property exists on these controls. Setting it via code-behind compiles and runs without error. But the text color doesn't change.

---

## What Doesn't Work

### 1. Direct Property Setting via Code-Behind

```csharp
// Walking the visual tree and setting Foreground
if (parent is Fluent.Button fluentButton)
{
    fluentButton.Foreground = new SolidColorBrush(Colors.White);
}
else if (parent is Fluent.DropDownButton dropDown)
{
    dropDown.Foreground = new SolidColorBrush(Colors.White);
}
else if (parent is Fluent.SplitButton splitButton)
{
    splitButton.Foreground = new SolidColorBrush(Colors.White);
}
```

**Result:** No effect. The property is set, but text remains black.

### 2. Setting Foreground on Child Text Elements

```csharp
// Trying to reach the actual text elements
if (parent is TextBlock textBlock)
{
    textBlock.Foreground = foreground;
}
else if (parent is AccessText accessText)
{
    accessText.Foreground = foreground;
}
else if (parent is ContentPresenter contentPresenter)
{
    TextElement.SetForeground(contentPresenter, foreground);
}
```

**Result:** No effect. Template bindings override these settings.

### 3. TextElement.SetForeground Attached Property

```csharp
// Catch-all attempt using attached property
TextElement.SetForeground(element, foreground);
```

**Result:** No effect.

### 4. Overriding Fluent.Ribbon Resource Brushes

```csharp
// Trying to override the brushes Fluent.Ribbon uses internally
Application.Current.Resources["Fluent.Ribbon.Brushes.LabelTextBrush"] = whiteBrush;
Application.Current.Resources["Fluent.Ribbon.Brushes.IdealForegroundColorBrush"] = whiteBrush;
Application.Current.Resources["Fluent.Ribbon.Brushes.BlackBrush"] = whiteBrush;
```

**Result:** No effect. Internal templates use `StaticResource`, not `DynamicResource`.

### 5. ControlzEx.Theming.ThemeManager

```csharp
// Using the built-in theme manager
ControlzEx.Theming.ThemeManager.Current.ChangeTheme(this, "Dark.Blue");
// or
ControlzEx.Theming.ThemeManager.Current.ChangeTheme(Application.Current, "Dark.Blue");
```

**Result:** Changes accent colors but doesn't fix button text foreground.

---

## Why Nothing Works

Fluent.Ribbon button control templates are designed with:

1. **Internal template bindings** - The template controls text rendering, ignoring the `Foreground` property set externally
2. **StaticResource usage** - Internal brushes are resolved at load time, not dynamically
3. **Template-level triggers** - Visual states and triggers override external property values
4. **Sealed rendering logic** - Text elements inside the template are not accessible for theming via code

This is different from standard WPF controls or even the ribbon's structural elements (Panels, Borders) which DO respond to direct property setting via visual tree walk.

---

## The Solution

Add `Foreground` binding directly in XAML using `DynamicResource`:

```xml
<fluent:Button Foreground="{DynamicResource TextPrimaryBrush}"
               Header="My Button"
               Size="Large"
               Icon="{StaticResource MyIcon}"/>
```

### Why This Works

1. **DynamicResource** - Creates a live binding that updates when the theme changes
2. **XAML declaration** - Takes precedence over template defaults
3. **Explicit property** - The template respects explicitly declared properties in the element

---

## Complete Implementation

### Step 1: Define Theme Brushes

```xml
<!-- LightTheme.xaml -->
<SolidColorBrush x:Key="TextPrimaryBrush" Color="#212121" />
<SolidColorBrush x:Key="TextSecondaryBrush" Color="#757575" />

<!-- DarkTheme.xaml -->
<SolidColorBrush x:Key="TextPrimaryBrush" Color="#FFFFFF" />
<SolidColorBrush x:Key="TextSecondaryBrush" Color="#B0B0B0" />
```

### Step 2: Apply to All Ribbon Buttons

```xml
<fluent:RibbonGroupBox Header="File Operations">
    <fluent:Button Foreground="{DynamicResource TextPrimaryBrush}"
                   Header="Open"
                   Size="Large"
                   Icon="{StaticResource OpenIcon}"
                   Command="{Binding OpenCommand}"/>

    <fluent:Button Foreground="{DynamicResource TextPrimaryBrush}"
                   Header="Save"
                   Size="Large"
                   Icon="{StaticResource SaveIcon}"
                   Command="{Binding SaveCommand}"/>

    <fluent:SplitButton Foreground="{DynamicResource TextPrimaryBrush}"
                        Header="Export"
                        Size="Large"
                        Icon="{StaticResource ExportIcon}">
        <fluent:MenuItem Header="Export as PDF"/>
        <fluent:MenuItem Header="Export as CSV"/>
    </fluent:SplitButton>

    <fluent:DropDownButton Foreground="{DynamicResource TextPrimaryBrush}"
                           Header="Recent"
                           Size="Middle"
                           Icon="{StaticResource RecentIcon}">
        <fluent:MenuItem Header="File1.txt"/>
        <fluent:MenuItem Header="File2.txt"/>
    </fluent:DropDownButton>
</fluent:RibbonGroupBox>
```

### Step 3: Don't Forget Group Headers

If you use custom group header templates:

```xml
<DataTemplate x:Key="GroupHeaderWithSubtitle">
    <StackPanel HorizontalAlignment="Center">
        <TextBlock Text="{Binding}"
                   Foreground="{DynamicResource TextPrimaryBrush}"
                   HorizontalAlignment="Center"
                   FontSize="11"/>
        <TextBlock Text="{Binding RelativeSource={RelativeSource AncestorType=fluent:RibbonGroupBox}, Path=Tag}"
                   Foreground="{DynamicResource TextSecondaryBrush}"
                   FontSize="9"
                   Opacity="0.6"
                   HorizontalAlignment="Center"/>
    </StackPanel>
</DataTemplate>
```

### Step 4: Handle Mixed Controls

If you have standard WPF buttons alongside Fluent.Ribbon buttons:

```xml
<!-- Standard WPF Button also needs the binding -->
<Button Foreground="{DynamicResource TextPrimaryBrush}"
        Content="Load Cached Results"
        Command="{Binding LoadCachedCommand}"/>
```

---

## Key Insights

### 1. Two Different Theming Approaches

| Element Type | Theming Approach |
|-------------|------------------|
| Ribbon structure (tab row, panels, borders) | Visual tree walk with direct property setting |
| Declared controls (buttons, dropdowns) | XAML `DynamicResource` bindings |

### 2. Don't Fight the Framework

If setting a property via code-behind doesn't work, the answer is usually XAML. Fluent.Ribbon templates are designed to work with XAML declarations, not runtime property manipulation.

### 3. Visual Tree Walk Still Has Value

The visual tree walk approach works perfectly for:
- Tab row background colors
- Active/selected tab highlighting
- Border and panel backgrounds
- Internal structural elements

It just doesn't work for templated control text.

### 4. This is the Proper WPF Pattern

Using `DynamicResource` for theme-aware properties is the standard WPF approach. It's not a hack - it's how WPF theming is meant to work.

---

## Summary

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Button text black in dark mode | Add `Foreground="{DynamicResource TextPrimaryBrush}"` to XAML |
| Code-behind Foreground setting ignored | Use XAML binding instead |
| Group header text wrong color | Add Foreground binding to DataTemplate TextBlocks |

---

## Related Resources

- [Fluent.Ribbon Tab Row Theming Guide](./fluent-ribbon-theming-guide.md) - Tab row background customization
- [Fluent.Ribbon Active Tab Styling Guide](./fluent-ribbon-active-tab-styling-guide.md) - Selected tab differentiation
- [Fluent.Ribbon GitHub](https://github.com/fluentribbon/Fluent.Ribbon) - Official repository

---

## Version History

| Date | Fluent.Ribbon Version | Notes |
|------|----------------------|-------|
| 2026-01-10 | 10.0.4, 11.0.1 | Initial guide |

---

*This guide documents solutions discovered through extensive trial and error (10+ failed approaches). The fix is simple once you know it - the value is in knowing what doesn't work and why.*


  </details>

  ---

  *Tested with Fluent.Ribbon 10.0.4 and 11.0.1 on .NET 8.0 WPF*

When combined with WPF-UI theming library, button headers are too big (apparently the theming library manages to somehow force size of the labels) and overflow from buttons.

To reproduce: add WPF-UI library, configure it by adding to the App.xaml resources:

```
             xmlns:ui="http://schemas.lepo.co/wpfui/2022/xaml"

            <ResourceDictionary.MergedDictionaries>
                <ui:ThemesDictionary Theme="Light" />
                <ui:ControlsDictionary />
            </ResourceDictionary.MergedDictionaries>
```

Or turn on the new theming mechanism present since C#9:

```
<App (...) ThemeMode="Light" (...) />
```

Then add a button with two-line caption. The caption will be too big and will overflow from the button.

Obviously external libraries may interfere with how Fluent.Ribbon works, but maybe it might be a good idea to force the size of button header captions, since other elements of the UI are fixed too? Or even enforce (or template-bind) size of the font of all UI elements, so that it can be controlled from a central place?

body:
This was a real issue and we implented the fix that is described at the end as workaround. The following text ist completely created by Copilot (and checked by me for correct informations regarding error and workaround, if the fix works this way you have to test yourself).

**Summary**
After executing an ICommand via a Ribbon button, Keyboard.FocusedElement is set to null. This breaks WPF's internal focus-restore mechanism when a ShowDialog() call follows — after closing the dialog, the main window no longer accepts keyboard input.
**Technical Root Cause**
The Ribbon control is its own WPF FocusScope (FocusManager.IsFocusScope="True"). When a Fluent:Button is clicked and its ICommand executes, it releases keyboard focus — but Fluent Ribbon does not explicitly restore focus to the last focused element outside the Ribbon's FocusScope.
WPF's ShowDialog() internally saves Keyboard.FocusedElement before opening the dialog (as restoreFocusElement) in order to restore it after closing. If that value is null, the restoration silently fails:

_// WPF internals (simplified):_
IInputElement restoreFocusElement = Keyboard.FocusedElement;  // → null after Ribbon click
dialog.ShowDialog();
restoreFocusElement?.Focus();  // → null?.Focus() → no effect

The result: IsKeyboardFocusWithin = false on the RibbonWindow, PreviewKeyDown no longer routes, and all keyboard input is "swallowed" until the user presses Tab or clicks a focusable element.
**Comparison with Standard WPF ToolBar**
WPF's built-in ToolBar solves this explicitly: after a button click, the ToolBar returns focus to the previously focused element in the main content area. Fluent Ribbon is missing this logic.

**Minimal Reproduction**
_// In a RibbonWindow, Ribbon button with this command handler:_
private void MyRibbonButton_Executed(object sender, ExecutedRoutedEventArgs e)
{
    // After this ShowDialog() returns → keyboard input no longer works
    new MyDialog { Owner = this }.ShowDialog();
}

**Steps:**
1.	Start the application
2.	Click a Ribbon button → dialog opens
3.	Close the dialog (Escape / Cancel)
4.	Press any key → no event fires, keyboard input is swallowed
5.	Press Tab or click a button → keyboard input works again
**Expected Behavior**
After a command is executed via a Ribbon button, Keyboard.FocusedElement should point to a valid element in the main content area (analogous to ToolBar behavior).
**Suggested Fix in Fluent Ribbon**
In the click/command execution pipeline of Ribbon buttons, after ICommand.Execute(...):

_// Restore focus to the last focused element outside the Ribbon FocusScope:_
Window parentWindow = Window.GetWindow(this);
if (parentWindow != null && !parentWindow.IsKeyboardFocusWithin)
{
    parentWindow.MoveFocus(new TraversalRequest(FocusNavigationDirection.First));
}

Alternatively, RibbonWindow could override OnActivated and ensure the same — however, that is an application-level workaround, not a fix for the underlying issue.

---

## Environment

```Component: Fluent:Button / Fluent:RibbonWindow Version: 11.0.2 Platform: WPF / .NET 8```

body:
This is a general purpose fix for *all* possible missing QAT properties for `ItemsControl` & `Selector` based controls.

The quick access creation/binding logic seems quite fragmented in general.
A lot of logic happens in shared methods, then there are base class methods that bind some properties, omit others. Then there may be overloads that are extended COPIES of base implementations but that do not call the base versions.

All in all I'm not shocked that there are issues in there.

I _think_ at a minimum this could benefit from a cleanup where duplicated/repeated binds are eliminated and code is centralized.

---

To me the entire `IQuickAccessItemProvider.CreateQuickAccessItem()` logic smells like a poor man's attempt at templating/framework element factory replication. It knows how to create controls and set some linked states in them. But it does so in a fragmented, non-idiomatic and non-extensible way.

My gut instinct here is to say: That's fricken templating. Why not *implement* it as templating.

Every Fluent control that supports addition to QAT get's a 'QATTemplate' property of type `DataTemplate`. The QAT uses *that* as ItemTemplate per toolbar element. Each element's `DataContext` *is* the originating control. That should allow clean xaml based template definition & binding. Might need some custom Markupextension for some wiring (private event handlers in particular come to mind). Also there may be some shenanigans with logical child shuffling I'm not seeing clear enough.

But in general that would allow a cleaner XAML based (and thus idiomatic & extensible) approach to "What does this look like in the QAT"). Would allow reuse of (shared) styles for common properties and should allow way easier discovery of overlooked (or repeat used) links.
title: General purpose fix for missing/untransfered ItemsControl QAT properties
